newsitem.title: USA: Green groups battle to protect parks in aid bill.
newsitem.headline: Green groups battle to protect parks in aid bill.

text.p: Green groups Thursday kept up pressure on the Clinton administration to veto a disaster aid bill if it included a provision that would potentially let states build roads in national parks and wildlife refuges.

Clinton earlier this week told Republican leaders he would veto the bill unless lawmakers dropped a proposal to allow states to build roads on footpaths, dogsled trails and other old state transport routes on public lands.

But environmentalists feared that if Congress backed down on other measures that the administration opposed in the disaster aid bill, Clinton might let the roadbuilding proposal stand, said Ben Beach, spokesman for the Wilderness Society.

The amendment was a key obstacle to an agreement in Congress on an $8.4 billion disaster aid bill, and forced lawmakers to give up trying to pass the broad bill before breaking for a week-long recess.

The measure is being pushed by Senate Appropriations Chairman Sen. Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, who says his state wants to build on the old rights of way because native villages need good roads to link them to schools and other public services.

"Americans simply do not believe that our most spectacular lands should be bulldozed to create more roads," said Wilderness Society president William Meadows, pointing to a survey done for the group showing that 70 percent of voters opposed the measure.
A group of Republican lawmakers earlier this week wrote to House Appropriations Chairman Representative Bob Livingston, a Louisiana Republican, urging him to oppose the controversial amendment.

"A disaster relief bill is not the proper forum to adequately scrutinise and debate land-use policy with wide ranging impacts," the 17 Republicans, led by Connecticut Representative Christopher Shays, said in May 20 letter released by the Alaska Wilderness League.
"We believe that the RS 2477 rider (amendment) should not be part of this legislation," they said.
